organizingIdeas.title: Number
organizingIdeas.statement: Quantity is measured with numbers that enable counting, labelling, comparing, and operating.

guidingQuestions.question: How can quantity contribute meaning to daily life?

knowledge.text: Quantity can be represented by using

understanding.text: Quantity can be the number of objects in a set.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Recognize a number of familiar objects as a quantity.
Represent a quantity in different ways.
Relate a numeral to a specific quantity.

knowledge.text: Quantity can be determined by counting.

understanding.text: A quantity is always counted by using the same sequence of words (counting principle: stable order).
A quantity remains the same no matter the order in which the objects are counted (counting principle: order irrelevance).
A quantity can be determined by counting each object in a set once and only once (counting principle: one-to-one correspondence).
The last number used to count represents the quantity (counting principle: cardinality).
Any quantity of like or unlike objects can be counted as a set (counting principle: abstraction).

skillsAndProcedures.text: Count within 10, forward and backward, starting at any number, according to the counting principles.

knowledge.text: A small quantity can be recognized at a glance (subitized).

understanding.text: Quantity can be determined without counting.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Subitize quantities to 5.

knowledge.text: Comparisons of quantity can be described by using words such as

understanding.text: A quantity can be described relative to another quantity.
A quantity can be described in relation to a purpose or need.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Compare the size of two sets, using one-to-one correspondence.
Describe quantities relative to each other, using comparative language.
Describe a quantity in relation to a purpose or need, using comparative language.
Solve problems in familiar situations by counting.

guidingQuestions.question: In what ways can quantity be composed?

outcomes.outcome: Children interpret compositions of quantities within 10.

knowledge.text: Quantity can be arranged in various ways.

understanding.text: A quantity remains the same no matter how the objects are grouped or arranged (counting principle: conservation).

skillsAndProcedures.text: Identify a quantity in various groups or arrangements.
Compose quantities within 10.
Recognize various ways to make 5 and 10.

organizingIdeas.title: Geometry
organizingIdeas.statement: Shapes are defined and related by geometric attributes.

guidingQuestions.question: How can shape bring meaning to the space in an environment?

knowledge.text: A shape can be represented by using objects, pictures, or words.
Familiar two- and three-dimensional shapes can be found in nature, such as
First Nations, Métis, and Inuit relate specific shapes to those found in nature.

understanding.text: Shape is structured two-dimensional or three-dimensional space.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Relate shapes in nature to various two-dimensional and three-dimensional shapes.
Identify familiar two- and three-dimensional shapes.
Investigate three-dimensional shapes by rolling, stacking, or sliding.
Describe a shape, using words such as flat, curved, straight, or round.

organizingIdeas.title: Measurement
organizingIdeas.statement: Attributes such as length, area, volume, and angle are quantified by measurement.

guidingQuestions.question: In what ways can size be distinguished?

outcomes.outcome: Children explore size through direct comparison.

knowledge.text: Size can be interpreted in many ways (according to measurable attributes), such as
items: how much flat space an object covers (area)

understanding.text: Size describes the amount of one measurable attribute of an object or a space.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Identify measurable attributes of familiar objects to which size may refer.

knowledge.text: Comparisons of size can be described by using words such as

understanding.text: Size may refer to only one measurable attribute at a time.
The size of two objects can be compared directly.
The size of an object can be described in relation to a purpose or need.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Compare the length, area, weight, or capacity of two objects directly.
Describe the size of an object in relation to another object, using comparative language.
Describe the size of an object in relation to a purpose or need, using comparative language.

organizingIdeas.title: Patterns
organizingIdeas.statement: Awareness of patterns supports problem solving in various situations.

outcomes.outcome: Children identify and create repeating patterns.

knowledge.text: A pattern can involve elements such as
Repeating patterns have one or more elements that repeat.

understanding.text: A pattern is characterized by how the elements change or remain constant.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Recognize repeating patterns encountered in daily routines and play, including songs or dances.
Recognize change or constancy between elements in a repeating pattern.
Predict the next elements in a repeating pattern.
Create a repeating pattern with up to three repeating elements.

organizingIdeas.title: Time
organizingIdeas.statement: Duration is described and quantified by time.

guidingQuestions.question: In what ways can time be described?

outcomes.outcome: Children interpret time as a sequence of events.

knowledge.text: Sequence in time can be described in words, such as
Ordinal numbers can indicate order in time.

understanding.text: Time can be perceived as a sequence.
